EDU-Jev: Training System-One Decision Models
for Education
Jiazheng Li     Yulan He
King’s College London

{jiazheng.li, yulan.he}@kcl.ac.uk

October 2026

Abstract

Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass (“System One”) decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.

1  Introduction

Educational assessment involves many small decisions: assigning a short answer 0 to 3 marks under a rubric, rating an essay on several traits, checking whether a marking point is present or absent, identifying the first incorrect step in a solution, or judging whether a tutor’s reply is appropriate. In most cases, the allowed outcomes are fixed in advance. Automated scoring has addressed such decisions for decades [42, 2, 6, 23], and its operational requirements are well established: agreement with human markers, consistency across responses, and confidence estimates reliable enough to route uncertain cases to a person [55]. Feedback is also most useful when learners receive it while still working on a task [4, 20, 50]. As LLM-based systems increasingly generate feedback with educators in the loop [62], cost and response time become part of the educational challenge.

Large language models are often used for these tasks as generative judges that write a rationale followed by a verdict [64]. In assessment, this approach includes explainable scoring systems that justify each mark against a rubric [28, 30, 31, 32]. Reasoning models and inference-time reflection extend this process with additional deliberation [54, 18, 34]. For assessment, however, this deliberate, “System Two” [22] approach has three drawbacks. First, generated outputs require parsing and may fall outside the allowed options, while their rationales may not faithfully reflect how the decision was reached [33]. Second, inference cost grows with output length, and reasoning models can generate many tokens even for simple decisions [7]. Third, their verbalised confidence does not by itself provide a calibrated probability [17]. Moreover, the benefits of chain-of-thought reasoning are mainly on mathematical and symbolic tasks, with smaller gains on other tasks [51]. Most assessment decisions, by contrast, involve judging a response against a given rubric rather than multi-step symbolic reasoning.

A single-pass (“System One”) decision model offers a direct way to make such judgements. It takes a context and a question with a specified answer type and predefined options, then returns a probability distribution over those options in one forward pass. This design restricts outputs to valid choices, avoids autoregressive decoding, and allows probabilities to be trained directly using an objective that encourages calibration. This typed-decision interface was introduced by TypeSafe AI with its hosted decision model Jev [1], which we evaluate through the version 1.14 API. JevBench [3] is an independent public benchmark for such models. We refer to open models that implement the same interface as Jev-style models [49, 25, 39, 13, 43]. They are trained primarily on general decision data and, as our evaluation shows, are weak on rubric-based assessment. The challenge is to improve their assessment capabilities while retaining valid outputs, efficient inference, and an objective that supports reliable probability estimates.

We introduce EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass decision models for educational assessment. Each model reads an assessment context, such as the item, rubric, reference answer or key points, student response, solution steps, or tutoring dialogues, and answers a choice, score, or yes/no question. Instead of the language-model output head, a pointer head reads one hidden state per option and returns a distribution over exactly the declared options (Section 2). What changes relative to general decision models is mainly the training data: a broad mixture of assessment tasks that provide information a human marker would need, including the question and its rubric, reference answer, or key points [56].

EDU-Jev is trained from Qwen3.5 base models [45] in a single supervised stage on about 1.5B tokens of typed decisions, with a strictly proper loss on soft labels and model souping (Section 3). We evaluate the 0.8B, 2B and 4B models against open Jev-style models, zero-shot Qwen3.5 models, and five commercial decision APIs on a 20-set suite that separates general decisions, reasoning, and education within and across domains, with every model scored on the same items (Sections 4 and 5). The 4B model achieves an average accuracy of 67.6% across the twelve education benchmarks, compared with 45.2–48.9% for open 4B decision models and 49.2–58.2% for commercial APIs (Figure 1). The 2B (63.2%) and 0.8B (62.8%) models also outperform all evaluated baselines on the education average. On the four cross-domain education sets, the 4B model matches the strongest API. It trails the APIs by 3.2 to 6.7 percentage points on general decisions and trails three of them by 2.2 to 3.7 percentage points on reasoning.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We introduce EDU-Jev, a family of 0.8B, 2B and 4B single-pass decision models for education. Their pointer readout restricts predictions to the declared answer options by construction.

  • •

    We describe a compact supervised recipe and show which choices mattered: broad data coverage, learning-rate decay while training on unseen data, and model souping. We also show that reinforcement learning on the pointer readout does not beat continued supervised training, and analyse the reasons for this result (Section 6).

  • •

    We show that EDU-Jev 4B has the highest average accuracy across the education benchmarks among all compared models, exceeding the strongest commercial API by 9.4 percentage points. In the matched-data comparisons, increasing model size produces larger gains on several transfer and general-reasoning measures than on in-domain assessment accuracy (Sections 5.1 and 5.2).

2  Approach

2.1  Typed decisions

A decision instance is a triple x=(s,u,𝒪)x=(s,u,\mathcal{O}). The state ss is a small set of named text fields: the item, a rubric, a reference answer or key points, the student response, solution steps, a tutoring dialogue or a passage. Fields that describe provenance (dataset, split, label source) are never shown to the model. The question uu has instructions and a type τ∈{choice,score,yes/no}\tau\in\{\textsc{choice},\textsc{score},\textsc{yes/no}\}, and 𝒪=(o1,…,oK)\mathcal{O}=(o_{1},\dots,o_{K}) are its options. The three types share the input format and the readout and differ only in a type tag in the input and in what the options are: unordered alternatives for choice (2≤K≤2552\leq K\leq 255, e.g. the first erroneous step or a misconception), ordered levels with numeric values v1<⋯<vKv_{1}<\dots<v_{K} for score (2≤K≤102\leq K\leq 10, e.g. 0 to 6 marks or an essay band), and the pair (yes, no) for a binary proposition such as “the response makes marking point 3”.

The target is a distribution q∈ΔK−1q\in\Delta^{K-1}: the rater histogram when several raters are available, otherwise one-hot. The model returns pθ(⋅∣x)∈ΔK−1p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\in\Delta^{K-1}. From this distribution we derive the predicted option k^=arg⁡maxk⁡pk\hat{k}=\arg\max_{k}p_{k}, a confidence score 1−H⁡(p)/log⁡K1-H(p)/\log K, where HH is the Shannon entropy, and, for score questions, the expected score ∑kpk​vk\sum_{k}p_{k}v_{k}. Several questions about one response (several traits or marking points) share the state. Scoring questions are accepted only when ss contains the item and at least one of rubric, reference answer or key points; we neither train nor serve answer-only scoring.

2.2  Single forward pass with a pointer head

The input is serialised as text in a fixed order: the state fields, the question, then each option followed by a dedicated marker token, and finally a decision token (Figure 2). One causal forward pass of the decoder gives hidden states h1,…,hK∈ℝdh_{1},\dots,h_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at the option markers and g∈ℝdg\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at the decision token. A two-layer MLP ϕ\phi, shared across options, scores each option, and a softmax over exactly the KK logits of the question gives the output:

zk=ϕ([hk;g;hk⊙g]),pθ(k∣x)=exp⁡zk∑j=1Kexp⁡zj,k=1,…,K.z_{k}=\phi\big([\,h_{k};\;g;\;h_{k}\odot g\,]\big),\qquad p_{\theta}(k\mid x)=\frac{\exp z_{k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp z_{j}},\qquad k=1,\dots,K. (1)

The readout points at input positions, as in pointer networks [53], and the language-model head is not used. Two consequences follow. The output is typed by construction: the model can be wrong only by choosing badly, never by producing an unparseable or out-of-range answer. Each display order requires one prefill forward pass, without autoregressive answer generation. The number of passes does not increase with the number of options, but computational cost increases with the total input length, including the option text. Prefix caching can reuse the shared state across questions or display orders where their serialised prefixes coincide.

We chose this readout in controlled 0.8B comparisons (three seeds each, paired soft cross-entropy on held-out validation questions; lower is better). A letter head that reads the language-model logits of option labels “A/B/C”, the usual readout for multiple-choice evaluation [21, 47], was significantly worse (+0.033+0.033) and agreed less often across option orders (by 3.5 points), in line with the label and position biases of letter readouts [63, 44]. Of the other heads we tried, including set attention across the option states [27], only mean pooling over the option span [46] was significantly worse; the rest, and starting from the instruction-tuned rather than the pre-trained base checkpoint, were within noise. We therefore start from the base checkpoint.

2.3  Soft-label training with a proper scoring rule

The training loss is the soft cross-entropy

ℒ(θ)=𝔼(x,q)[−∑k=1Kqklogpθ(k∣x)],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,q)}\Big[-\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}\log p_{\theta}(k\mid x)\Big], (2)

a strictly proper scoring rule [16]: for each xx its expectation is uniquely minimised by p=qp=q. This strict-propriety property makes cross-entropy an appropriate objective for learning the target label distribution. Where human raters disagree, qq preserves their observed disagreement. In our evaluated ablations, adding a Brier or ranked-probability term for ordinal questions did not improve the reported metrics, so we retain cross-entropy alone.

2.4  Order-averaged evaluation

Predictions should be robust to arbitrary changes in option display order. During training the option order and the surface formatting of the input are randomised. At evaluation each question is presented under a set Π⁡(x)\Pi(x) of display orders (on internal held-out sets, four orders for choice and both directions for yes/no and score; on the benchmark suite, two orders per question); the predictions are mapped back to the canonical order and averaged,

p¯​(k∣x)=1|Π⁡(x)|​∑π∈Π⁡(x)pθ​(π⁡(k)∣π⁡(x)),\bar{p}(k\mid x)=\frac{1}{|\Pi(x)|}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi(x)}p_{\theta}\big(\pi(k)\mid\pi(x)\big), (3)

and every metric is computed from p¯\bar{p}. We also report order consistency, the fraction of questions whose arg-max is the same under every π∈Π⁡(x)\pi\in\Pi(x). Single-order evaluation can be misleading, because a model that has learned only position or label priors can look strong in the original order; on our internal held-out sets every model is therefore also compared with a per-unit label-prior baseline on the same rows.

2.5  Model souping

We save weights θt\theta_{t} at one half and three quarters of a run of TT steps and at its end, and use their uniform average [57] as the final model

θ¯=13​(θT/2+θ3​T/4+θT).\bar{\theta}=\tfrac{1}{3}\big(\theta_{T/2}+\theta_{3T/4}+\theta_{T}\big). (4)

Averaging costs no training and, in our runs, trades at most a few tenths of a point of in-distribution accuracy for about one point of out-of-distribution accuracy (Section 6).

3  Training

3.1  Recipe

All models are trained in a single supervised stage from Qwen3.5 base checkpoints [45] at 0.8B, 2B and 4B. Qwen3.5 is a hybrid decoder in which most layers are linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers and every fourth layer uses full attention; we use only the text backbone. All parameters are trained (full fine-tuning), the pointer head with a larger learning rate than the backbone, and the learning rate decreases with model size. Training sequences pack several decision instances into one sequence with exact per-instance isolation, including the recurrent state of the linear-attention layers.

The learning-rate schedule is warmup-stable-decay (WSD) [19]: a short linear warmup, a long constant phase and a final decay. One detail turned out to matter: the decay phase reads data the model has not seen before, namely the tail of the epoch, rather than starting a second pass over seen data (Section 6). Each model is trained for one epoch of the mixture, about 1.5B tokens or 4.6M decision instances, at a global batch of about 131k tokens per step; the 4B model uses fully sharded data parallelism. We use model souping for the final weights, Equation (4).

3.2  Data

The training mixture combines public educational and NLP datasets, programmatically generated tasks, and synthetic items and labels produced by third-party models (Section 9). The educational sources cover short-answer scoring, essay and learner-text scoring, step-level verification of worked solutions, student-error remediation and tutoring dialogues. Every source is converted to the typed-decision format of Section 2 and assigned to a capability category. Figure 3 shows the approximate relative composition of the mixture. Scoring of free-text responses is split into short-answer scoring, essay holistic scoring, essay analytic-trait scoring and language-proficiency level; analytic-trait scoring is the largest of these, because one essay is scored on several traits. The data are mostly English and Chinese, with smaller amounts of other languages (for example German, Portuguese and learner texts in several European languages).

Within the educational categories, sources are balanced by a temperature over task families and capped per item so that no single question is repeated more than a few times per epoch. Labels come at several quality tiers (multi-rater human, single human, rule-exact, model-generated); all tiers are used with equal weight. Only rows whose context contains what a human marker would need are used for scoring decisions. Openly licensed sources include SciEntsBank and Beetle [12], SAF [14], MERLIN [5], PRM800K [36], MR-GSM8K [61], student-error remediation data [11], MathDial [38], CIMA [52] and MRBench [40] (CC BY, CC BY-SA or MIT licences); other sources are used under their respective terms (Section 9).

3.3  Decontamination

Training, validation and test splits are made at the level of content clusters. Items are grouped by exact match after text normalisation and by near-duplicate detection (MinHash signatures over character 5-grams with locality-sensitive hashing), and a cluster never crosses splits. All training data are then screened against every evaluation set used in this report, including the external benchmarks, by exact match, 8-gram overlap and MinHash near-duplicate detection on the item text, and matching training rows are removed. Source evaluation splits, and public test sets whose items circulate in other training corpora (for example grade-school and competition mathematics), are kept as block lists, so that copies inside other sources are caught by the same tests. Benchmarks that belong to task families represented in training are kept but reported separately as in-domain, and the problem-solving benchmark is reported on its subset of items with low n-gram overlap with the training data (Section 4).

4  Evaluation

4.1  Metrics

The primary metric is accuracy: the arg-max of the order-averaged distribution p¯\bar{p} (Equation (3)) against the gold label (for multi-rater items, the official gold or the majority). For ordinal scoring tasks we also report quadratic weighted kappa [10], computed per question or prompt and averaged. For KK ordered levels, with Oi​jO_{ij} the number of items with gold level ii and predicted level jj, Ei​jE_{ij} the count expected from the two marginal distributions, and wi​j=(i−j)2/(K−1)2w_{ij}=(i-j)^{2}/(K-1)^{2},

QWK=1−∑i,jwi​j​Oi​j∑i,jwi​j​Ei​j.\mathrm{QWK}=1-\frac{\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}O_{ij}}{\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}E_{ij}}. (5)

Calibration [17, 29, 35], which matters for routing uncertain cases to a person [55], is measured by the expected calibration error over 15 equal-width bins B1,…,B15B_{1},\dots,B_{15} of the top-option probability,

ECE=∑b=115|Bb|N​|acc⁡(Bb)−conf⁡(Bb)|,\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{15}\frac{|B_{b}|}{N}\,\big|\mathrm{acc}(B_{b})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{b})\big|, (6)

where NN is the number of questions, acc⁡(Bb)\mathrm{acc}(B_{b}) the accuracy and conf⁡(Bb)\mathrm{conf}(B_{b}) the mean top probability in bin bb. ECE and soft cross-entropy are secondary metrics and are reported raw, at temperature 1, unless stated otherwise: temperatures fitted on in-distribution calibration data can hide over-confidence out of distribution. Confidence intervals are 95% paired bootstrap intervals that resample items within units (a unit is one dataset and question, e.g. one prompt and trait), with B=1000B=1000 resamples for the benchmark suite and B=2000B=2000 for comparisons on our internal held-out sets (Section 5.2). Differences we describe as significant have paired 95% bootstrap CIs excluding zero; we give point estimates in the text and mark the others as within noise or not significant. The intervals reflect item sampling only, not run-to-run variation (Section 7).

4.2  Benchmark suite

For comparison with other models we built a fixed suite of 20 sets, using only test or held-out splits, questions with at most 26 options, two display orders per question and unit-stratified samples of up to 1,500 questions. The sets are grouped by the ability they test.

  • •

    General decisions (5): a hard subset of the public MMDM benchmark [48] (MMDM-hard), the public split of JevBench [3], BoolQ [8], ARC-Challenge [9], and a transfer set of held-out general decision datasets such as WANLI [37].

  • •

    Reasoning (3): a problem-solving set of science and maths items (from ARC-Easy [9], OpenBookQA [41], high-school MMLU [21] and similar sources) restricted to low n-gram overlap with our training data, an in-family set of solving and answer-verification items, and held-out reading-comprehension questions from public datasets.

  • •

    Education, in-domain (8): held-out items of the education task families in EDU-Jev’s training data: short-answer scoring, essay scoring, rubric-point verification, step-level verification, error diagnosis, tutoring and classroom discourse, language assessment, and item analysis.

  • •

    Education, cross-domain (4): unseen prompts of known education datasets, unseen education datasets of known task families, short-answer scoring on unseen prompts of a public dataset (QWK), and short essay scoring on unseen prompts of a public dataset (QWK).

For EDU-Jev, the eight in-domain sets come from task families seen in training (with disjoint items), and the four cross-domain sets test prompts or datasets never seen in training. Cells of open third-party models carry flags taken from their public documentation: I the benchmark belongs to a task family in that model’s training data, P partly in-distribution, C contaminated (rewritten test items in training). The hosted APIs do not disclose their training data. Group averages are unweighted means of the benchmark accuracies; the education average covers both in-domain and cross-domain sets.

4.3  Baselines

We compare with the open Jev-style decision models we could run through their own published inference code (OpenJev-4B [49], JevK5-4B, JevK5-2B, Tev1-4B, AstroHan-4B, eve-rlcd-0.6B and kotoba-DeBERTa-0.4B; minimal compatibility fixes only)11 1 Hugging Face repositories: shenjunhao/OpenJev-4B, alibiserikbay/JevK5, alibiserikbay/JevK5-2B, togethercomputer/Tev1-4B-experimental, AstroHan/decision-head-qwen3.5-4b-rlcd-32k, anthonym21/qwen3-0.6b-rlcd-decision (eve-rlcd-0.6B), com-kotobalabs/open-jev-deberta-v3-large (kotoba-DeBERTa-0.4B), and Qwen/Qwen3.5-{0.8B,2B,4B}[-Base]. and with zero-shot Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B–4B, read out through the next-token probabilities of option letters averaged over display orders. We also query five commercial decision APIs through a routing service, using only endpoints with zero data retention. Section 9 notes why this comparison is not fully independent.

5  Results

All EDU-Jev numbers are for the final weight-averaged checkpoints. Unless noted, each configuration is a single training run.

5.1  Comparison with open decision models and hosted APIs

Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 1 summarise the comparison. All differences below are paired, for EDU-Jev 4B unless stated, in accuracy points (kappa points for QWK), and significant unless marked otherwise.

On education, EDU-Jev 4B has the highest average of all models (67.6), followed by our 2B (63.2) and 0.8B (62.8) models, so that every EDU-Jev model is above every other model in the comparison. The 4B model outperforms the strongest API, pplx-decider v1.2, by 9.4 points (67.6 vs. 58.2) and the other four APIs by 9.7 (Drex Max) to 18.3 points (Microsoft Decision-1), and it outperforms the open 4B models by 18.7 (OpenJev-4B) to 22.4 points (AstroHan-4B). Most of the lead comes from the eight in-domain families, where it is 13.6 (Drex Max) to 20.2 points (Microsoft Decision-1) over the APIs and 23.8 to 25.2 points over the open 4B models. The 4B model is best on seven of the eight in-domain sets, including families beyond response scoring such as error diagnosis, tutoring discourse and item analysis, and joint best (with our 2B model) on rubric-point verification.

On the four cross-domain education sets, the EDU-Jev 4B model achieves 55.2% average accuracy, compared with 55.4% for pplx-decider v1.2. The paired difference of −0.2-0.2 percentage points is not statistically significant. EDU-Jev 4B outperforms the other four APIs, by 1.8 (Drex Max) to 14.6 points (Microsoft Decision-1), and the open 4B models, by 7.4 to 16.8 points. It is far ahead on unseen prompts of known datasets (60.7 vs. at most 40.7 for open models and 47.9 for the APIs), and on short-answer scoring its QWK of 51.8 (41.4 at 2B) ranks third, behind zero-shot Qwen3.5-4B (54.5) and Microsoft Decision-1 (52.5), both differences within noise. It trails four of the five APIs on unseen datasets (66.8 vs. 69.8 to 72.3) and is level with Jev 1.14 there (68.7, not significant), and it trails pplx-decider v1.2 on short essay scoring (QWK 43.5 vs. 58.2), where it is level with OpenJev-4B (44.3) and Drex Max (43.9). The 2B model (46.0) is level with the strongest open 4B models on these sets (−1.9-1.9 against OpenJev-4B, not significant).

On reasoning, the 4B model (85.7) outperforms the open 4B models by 3.8 (OpenJev-4B) to 8.0 points (Tev1-4B) and is level with two APIs, Microsoft Decision-1 (+0.9+0.9) and Cloudflare Clef (+1.0+1.0), both within noise; it trails the other three APIs by 2.2 to 3.7 points. On general decisions, the 4B model (84.3) is level with JevK5-4B (+0.6+0.6, not significant), trails OpenJev-4B by 1.3 points, outperforms the zero-shot Qwen3.5-4B model by 6.3 points, and trails the five APIs by 3.2 to 6.7 points. JevBench is its largest gap to the open models (77.1 vs. 87.9 for the two strongest 4B models, one of which is flagged as contaminated).

These results show that EDU-Jev leads every compared model on education tasks of the kinds it was trained for, and that at 4B it carries much of that lead to unseen prompts and matches the strongest API on the cross-domain sets, while general decisions and reasoning, where broad pre-training matters more, remain the strength of the hosted APIs.

5.2  Scaling with model size

Table 3 lists the final models. All aggregate metrics shown in the table improve with model size, although improvements vary across measures and are not monotonic on every individual benchmark. To separate size from data, we compare models trained on identical data, schedule and token budget: a 2B model trained on the 0.8B model’s data for the first step, and the final 2B and 4B models, which share their data, for the second. Gains are paired and significant, except that solve and maths (small internal sets) are reported as point estimates only. From 0.8B to 2B the gain is small on in-distribution questions (+1.3+1.3), out of distribution (+1.6+1.6) and on the education average (+0.8+0.8), and larger on general decisions (+6.4+6.4) and on solving and maths (+9.1+9.1 each). From 2B to 4B the in-distribution gain is again small (+1.5+1.5), while out-of-distribution accuracy (+3.1+3.1), the education average (+4.4+4.4), general decisions (+6.2+6.2) and reasoning (+6.9+6.9) improve more; the education gain comes mostly from the cross-domain sets (+9.3+9.3, against +1.9+1.9 on the in-domain families). With three model sizes, we do not fit a scaling law. In these experiments, the increase from 2B to 4B produces larger gains on several transfer and general-reasoning measures than on in-domain assessment accuracy. The smaller in-domain gains are consistent with a data bottleneck; separating data and capacity limitations requires varying training-data volume at each model size.

Before each larger run we registered predictions with 80% intervals. For 0.8B to 2B, all endpoints fell inside them. For 2B to 4B, the change in validation soft cross-entropy (−0.045-0.045, predicted −0.043-0.043 with interval −0.055-0.055 to −0.031-0.031) and the held-out scoring QWK fell inside, and in-distribution accuracy was at the upper end, while the out-of-distribution, general and education gains were above their intervals: size helped beyond the training distribution more than we expected.

5.3  Serving efficiency

Because no tokens are generated, serving cost is one prefill per question and display order. We provide EDU-Jev through a model plugin for vLLM [26] that applies the pointer head as a pooling step, and through a direct PyTorch path; both reuse the training serialiser so that inputs are token-identical to training. On one H100 GPU, through the vLLM plugin, a 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second (corresponding to about 110k prompt tokens per second) on a realistic mix of request lengths at batch size 256, against about 120 per second for the direct path; for small batches the direct path is faster. Prefix caching gives a further 2.5–3.8×\times when many questions share a long state, such as several marking points of one response. Outputs match offline evaluation within the bf16 noise band: arg-max agreement with an fp32 reference is 99.3–99.6%, the same as the agreement between bf16 and fp32 inference in the reference implementation itself.

6  Analysis

The recipe of Section 3 was settled in controlled runs, mostly at 0.8B and 2B. This section summarises what mattered, what did not, and how well the output probabilities can be trusted.

6.1  What mattered

Data coverage gave the largest improvements, more than any change of architecture or objective. Problem-solving data (answering and verifying items) are a clear example: in a small-budget ablation, increasing their share improved maths solving by 13 points and answer verification by 6, without hurting in-distribution scoring. Before such data were added, judging a candidate answer without a reference was bounded by the model’s own ability to solve the item. More educational data also kept helping: at 2B, one full epoch raised in-distribution accuracy from 70.7% to 76.2% (final weights of a development run, before souping) over a run with a sixth of the tokens.

Running the learning-rate decay on unseen data mattered for generalisation. When the decay instead started a second pass over data the model had already seen, in-distribution metrics improved but raw out-of-distribution cross-entropy rose from 0.76 to 0.86 during the decay: confidence out of distribution grew while accuracy did not, and temperatures fitted on in-distribution data hid this. Decaying on the unseen tail of the epoch, from the same checkpoint and for the same number of steps, lowered raw out-of-distribution cross-entropy by 0.051 with in-distribution quality unchanged.

Model souping is a small but consistent trade. With the decay on unseen data the final weights are already good, and averaging the half, three-quarter and final checkpoints moves in-distribution accuracy by at most 0.3 points in either direction while adding 0.6 to 1.4 points out of distribution; at 4B the average is 0.5 points better out of distribution and 0.2 points lower in distribution than the final weights. Interpolating the backbone back towards its pre-trained weights [58] was dominated by model souping.

6.2  Calibration

Raw (temperature 1) calibration is good where the model has seen the task family and degrades outside it. On the benchmark suite the ECE of EDU-Jev 4B averages 0.043 on general decisions, 0.056 on reasoning and 0.044 on the in-domain education sets, lower than every hosted API on the in-domain sets (0.086 to 0.151) and lower than the best-calibrated open 4B model (JevK5-4B, 0.085). On the cross-domain education sets it rises to 0.161: within the range of the APIs (0.152 to 0.251) but worse than that model (0.110). The internal held-out sets show the same gradient, from 0.016 in distribution to 0.062 on transfer, 0.066 on unseen prompts and 0.125 on unseen datasets. Predictions are also stable under re-ordering: for the 2B model, the mean total-variation distance between the distributions for different display orders is 0.017 in distribution and 0.023 to 0.026 out of distribution, and 97% of in-distribution questions have the same arg-max in every order. These results suggest that the confidence can be used for routing within known task families, but should be re-checked on each new assessment.

6.3  What did not help

Reinforcement learning on the pointer readout, with actions sampled from the output distribution and rewarded by agreement with the label, did not beat continued supervised training in more than thirty controlled second-stage runs at 2B, across binary, ordinal and proper rewards and the usual regularisers. Binary-reward RL raised the mean top probability on validation from 0.80 to 0.98 while reducing accuracy by 0.8 to 1.2 percentage points. The reason is structural: for a single readout trained on labelled data, the expected policy gradient under a label-derived reward is a reweighted cross-entropy gradient (with a binary reward, pgoldp_{\text{gold}} times it), so such rewards add no information beyond the labels, and improper rewards push the output towards one-hot. This is consistent with the analysis of Wu et al. [59], who show that the supervised fine-tuning gradient is itself a policy gradient with an implicit reward, and with Gao and Wang [15], who prove that reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions cannot beat cross-entropy when the uncertainty comes from annotator disagreement; where reinforcement learning does improve classification, it acts on generated reasoning before the answer [60, 15]. We therefore keep a purely supervised recipe and reserve RL for generated reasoning (Section 8).

Training only the pointer head on a frozen backbone underfits badly (in-distribution accuracy 48% against 70% for full fine-tuning on the same budget), and larger heads or higher head learning rates do not close the gap, so full fine-tuning is required at these sizes. An abstention option trained on irrelevant option sets and richer pointer heads were neutral or worse.

7  Limitations

Alongside these results, the current models and evaluation have several limitations. First, generalisation to new assessments is incomplete. The strongest results are on task families represented in training, and the 4B model trails four of the five APIs on unseen datasets (66.8 vs. 69.8 to 72.3) and the strongest API on short essay scoring on unseen prompts (QWK 43.5 vs. 58.2); calibration is also weaker outside the training families. Users should therefore check agreement and calibration on a sample of marked responses for each new assessment, and adapt the model or route low-confidence cases to a teacher where needed. Second, eight of the twelve education benchmarks are held-out items of task families we train on, which, as far as their documentation discloses, the compared models were not specifically trained for, so part of the education lead reflects targeted training data; we report the in-domain and cross-domain groups separately for this reason and plan to extend the cross-domain sets. Third, EDU-Jev trails the hosted APIs on general decisions and three of them on reasoning, so it is best used as an assessment specialist rather than a general decision model; broader general-decision data are a natural next step. Fourth, each configuration is a single training run, and bootstrap intervals over items do not capture run-to-run variation, so small single-run differences on small benchmarks should be read with caution; multi-seed replicates of the main comparisons are planned. Finally, the models are text only (handwriting must be transcribed), are trained mostly on English and Chinese data, and have not been evaluated in a teacher-in-the-loop deployment; such a study, including an audit of differences across student populations, is required before operational use.

8  Conclusion and future work

EDU-Jev demonstrates that education-focused supervised training can produce small models that return structurally valid assessment decisions without autoregressive answer generation. Across twelve education evaluation sets, the 4B model achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated models, with its largest gains on task families represented in training. Its average accuracy across four cross-domain education sets is close to that of the strongest commercial decision API. The main priorities are to strengthen transfer, establish the reliability of confidence-based referral, and isolate the contributions of the training mixture and pointer readout through matched-data comparisons.

One direction is to let the model reason before making its decisions. An optional reasoning stage could generate a rationale before the answer options are processed, allowing the same rationale to be reused across display orders. With a reasoning budget of zero, the model would reduce to the current single-pass design. Reinforcement learning could optimise this stage by rewarding rationales that improve the pointer’s predictions under a proper scoring rule. Applying reinforcement learning directly to the readout did not improve performance in our experiments. Teacher-generated marking-point annotations could provide initial supervision for rationale generation. A second direction is to strengthen data and evaluation. Scaling from 2B to 4B produced the largest gains where the 2B model was weakest, with more modest improvements on in-domain task families. This pattern motivates investigating whether broader coverage and higher-quality supervision can improve performance on these families. Multi-seed replicates and evaluation on further assessment datasets and essay prompts are also needed to establish the robustness of the main comparisons.

9  Statements

Intended use

EDU-Jev is a research model for assisting assessment: marking short and extended responses against a given rubric, checking marking points, verifying solution steps, and flagging uncertain cases for human review. It is meant to be used with the item and its rubric, reference answer or key points in the context, and our serving code rejects scoring requests without them. It is not intended for high-stakes decisions about individual students without human oversight. Calibrated confidence is meant to support routing uncertain responses to a teacher, and should be re-checked on each new assessment before it is relied on. Automated scoring can be biased across student populations, languages and writing styles; we have not audited such effects.

Data and ethics

The training mixture combines public educational and NLP datasets (about 44% of training tokens under permissive or share-alike licences, and some without a stated licence), programmatically generated tasks, and synthetic items and labels produced by third-party models, including a commercial decision API. We excluded sources whose terms we read as forbidding model training; for third-party model outputs, terms of use may restrict downstream use, which is one reason the models are intended for research only. The public evaluation benchmarks (MMDM, JevBench, BoolQ, ARC, OpenBookQA, MMLU, WANLI) are used under their MIT, CC BY-SA, CC BY or Apache-2.0 licences.

Independence of the comparison

The comparison with open Jev-style models and hosted APIs is not fully independent: our general decision data include publicly released typed-decision training data of the kind some of these models were trained on, as well as synthetic labels from third-party decision models; conversely, several open models and all hosted APIs do not disclose their training data.

AI assistance

Code, experiments and drafts of this report were produced with the assistance of an AI coding agent working under the direction of the authors, who designed the studies, set the decision rules and reviewed the results. All numbers are taken from logged experiment outputs.

Appendix A Full benchmark results

Table 4 gives the group averages of every model in the comparison with their 95% bootstrap CIs, which resample items within units (B=1000B=1000); per-benchmark results for selected models are in Tables 1 and 2. Each question is shown in two display orders and the predictions are averaged. Every model, including the hosted APIs, is scored on the same items. Third-party models were run through their own published inference code with minimal compatibility fixes (dependency checks, maximum question length, truncation of over-long states); a few inputs beyond a model’s context limit were truncated in the middle of the state.

Appendix B Evaluation protocol details

On the internal held-out sets, choice questions are evaluated in four distinct orders (original, reversed and two seeded random orders; fewer when KK is small), yes/no questions with either answer first, and score questions in ascending and descending order. Option labels, when shown, are attached after permutation. For each question, we map predictions from every display order back to canonical option identities and average the probability distributions. Accuracy, cross-entropy and calibration metrics are then computed from this averaged distribution, and QWK is computed from the resulting predicted categories across questions. We do not average the separately computed metrics of the display-order variants.

Every model is also compared on these sets with a label-prior baseline: the mean training label of the same item or dataset, per option identity. A model that has learned only these priors can look strong in the original order, so development decisions were made on paired differences against this baseline.

Micro averages weight questions; macro averages weight units (dataset ×\times question) within families and then families. On the benchmark suite, QWK is computed per unit with at least 15 items and then averaged. Comparisons on the internal held-out sets use a paired bootstrap over units and items within units (B=2000B=2000); benchmark-suite tables and differences use B=1000B=1000. Where a decision rule or a predicted effect was fixed before a run (model size, learning rate, reinforcement-learning variants), it is reported as such, and deviations are stated in the text. The final checkpoint (the average of the half, three-quarter and final weights) was chosen by a rule fixed in advance, which combined in-distribution accuracy, out-of-distribution accuracy and a held-out scoring QWK.
